title: Serving many requests with a thread pool
summary: Why one slow request blocks a single-threaded server, why a thread per connection does not scale, and how to build the book's ThreadPool step by step: the API first, workers that own JoinHandles, a channel of boxed FnOnce jobs, a receiver shared through Arc<Mutex<...>>, and the while let trap that keeps a lock held for the whole job.

blocks.md: Our server handles one connection at a time. That is fine until one request is slow: the book adds a `/sleep` route that waits five seconds before answering, and while it sleeps, every other visitor waits too. Below, `/sleep` waits half a second, a second client asks for `/` shortly after, and we measure how long the fast request takes, first with one thread and then with a new thread per connection.

blocks.output:
one thread: / took more than 300 ms: true
thread per connection: / took less than 200 ms: true
blocks.explain: With one thread, `/` waits in the operating system's accept queue until `/sleep` is done. A thread per connection fixes that, but nothing limits the number of threads: a burst of 10,000 requests would create 10,000 threads and could exhaust the machine (a cheap denial-of-service attack).

blocks.title: A pool of threads
blocks.md:
A **thread pool** is a fixed group of threads waiting for work. The server hands each connection to the pool; a free thread takes it; when all threads are busy, new work waits in a queue. The number of threads, and so the load on the machine, has an upper bound, and up to N requests are served at the same time. (Other designs exist: the fork/join model, the single-threaded async I/O model of chapter 17, or the multithreaded async model that `tokio` uses.)

The book builds the pool with **compiler-driven development**: write the code you wish you could write, then fix the compiler errors one by one. The code we wish for looks almost like the thread-per-connection version:

blocks.explain: `ThreadPool` goes in the library crate (`src/lib.rs`) so `main.rs` can `use hello::ThreadPool;`. `execute` should take a closure exactly like `thread::spawn` does.

blocks.title: Building ThreadPool, one compiler error at a time

steps.title: new: validate the size
steps.md: A pool with zero threads makes no sense, so `new` asserts and documents the panic. The book also suggests a `build` function returning `Result<ThreadPool, PoolCreationError>`, which the exercise asks you to write.

steps.title: execute: copy thread::spawn's bounds
steps.md: `thread::spawn` takes `F: FnOnce() -> T + Send + 'static`. A request is handled once (`FnOnce`), on another thread (`Send`), which may outlive the caller (`'static`). We return nothing, so `T` is `()`.

steps.title: Workers own the threads
steps.md: `thread::spawn` wants code to run immediately, but pool threads must start empty and wait. So each thread is wrapped in a `Worker` with an `id` and the `JoinHandle<()>`. `new` creates `size` workers in a `Vec::with_capacity(size)`.

steps.title: A channel carries jobs
steps.md: The pool keeps the `Sender`; the workers need the `Receiver`. A **job** is a boxed closure, a trait object (chapter 18), because each closure has its own type.

steps.title: Share one receiver
steps.md: A channel has a single consumer, so passing `receiver` to four workers fails: it moves into the first. Share it with `Arc` (several owners) and a `Mutex` (one worker takes a job at a time).

steps.title: The worker loop
steps.md: Each worker loops: lock the mutex, wait for a job, release the lock, run the job. `execute` boxes the closure and sends it.

blocks.explain: The step before `Arc<Mutex<...>>`: the first loop iteration moves the receiver into worker 0. Rust's channels are multiple-producer, single-consumer, and the type system enforces it.

blocks.title: The whole pool
blocks.md: Here is the pool assembled, with a demo that sends six jobs of 100 ms each to three workers. Each job reports which thread ran it through a second channel. One line goes beyond the book's version at this point: a worker leaves its loop when `recv` fails, which happens once the pool is gone. Lesson 3 explains why that matters.

blocks.output:
jobs finished: [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
threads used: 3
about 200 ms instead of 600: true
blocks.explain: Three workers run six 100 ms jobs in two rounds. `rx.iter()` ends when every `tx` clone has been dropped, that is, after the last job. In the server, `pool.execute(|| handle_connection(stream))` is all `main` needs.

blocks.title: Why not while let?
blocks.md: It is tempting to write the worker loop as `while let Ok(job) = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv() { job(); }`. It compiles and it is wrong. With `let job = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv().unwrap();` the temporary `MutexGuard` is dropped **at the end of the `let` statement**, so the lock is free while the job runs. In `while let` (and `if let` and `match`), temporaries in the condition live **until the end of the block**, so the worker holds the lock during `job()` and the other workers cannot even receive. The pool then runs one job at a time. The playground below lets you measure it.

blocks.title: Find the lock that never lets go
blocks.md: Four workers, four jobs of 200 ms each: they should finish together in about 200 ms. With the `while let` loop they take 800 ms. Rewrite the worker loop so the `MutexGuard` is dropped before the job runs.
blocks.task: Print `4 jobs of 200 ms took less than 500 ms: true`.
blocks.expected_output: 4 jobs of 200 ms took less than 500 ms: true
hints: Receive in a `let` statement of its own: `let message = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv();`.
Then `match message { Ok(job) => job(), Err(_) => break }` inside a `loop`.

blocks.title: Build the ThreadPool
blocks.goal: Write the book's ThreadPool yourself, with the fallible constructor the book suggests as an extension.
blocks.behavior:
- `PoolCreationError::ZeroThreads`, with `Display` text `a thread pool needs at least one thread`, and `impl std::error::Error`.
- `ThreadPool::build(size) -> Result<ThreadPool, PoolCreationError>`: an error for 0, otherwise a pool with `size` worker threads.
- `ThreadPool::new(size)`: the same, but panics for 0.
- `size(&self) -> usize`: the number of workers.
- `execute(&self, f)` for any `F: FnOnce() + Send + 'static`: the job runs on one of the pool's threads, and up to `size` jobs run at the same time.
- A worker leaves its loop when the channel is closed, without panicking.
hints: Fields: `workers: Vec<Worker>` and `sender: mpsc::Sender<Job>` with `type Job = Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>;`.
In the worker: `let message = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv();` on its own line, then match on it; never `while let` with the lock in the condition.
blocks.solution_explain: The pool is a `Sender` plus workers that share one `Receiver` through `Arc<Mutex<...>>`. Taking the job in its own `let` statement releases the lock before the job runs, which is what lets the barrier test pass. `build` returns a typed error that implements `Error`, so callers can use `?` with it, while `new` keeps the book's panicking API on top of it.

questions.q: What is the main problem with spawning a thread per connection?
options: There is no limit, so a flood of requests can exhaust the machine
It is slower than one thread
questions.explanation: The pool bounds the number of threads.

questions.q: Why is a job `Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send + 'static>`?
options: Every closure has its own type, so a trait object lets one channel carry them all
questions.explanation: A channel has one element type.

questions.q: Why is the receiver wrapped in `Arc<Mutex<...>>`?
options: Several workers own it (Arc) and only one may take a job at a time (Mutex)

questions.q: Why does `while let Ok(job) = receiver.lock().unwrap().recv()` serialize the pool?
options: The MutexGuard lives until the end of the loop body, so the lock is held while the job runs
questions.explanation: A let statement drops its temporaries at its end; while let keeps them for the block.
Run once, on another thread, with no borrowed data.

points: One slow request blocks a single-threaded server; a thread per connection has no upper bound.
A thread pool runs at most N jobs at once and queues the rest.
Design the API first (new, execute) and let compiler errors guide the implementation.
Workers own JoinHandles and share one Receiver<Job> through Arc<Mutex<...>>; jobs are boxed FnOnce trait objects.
Receive in a plain let so the MutexGuard is dropped before the job runs; while let would hold it.

terms.def: A fixed set of threads that take tasks from a shared queue.
One thread of the pool together with its id; it loops taking and running jobs.
A unit of work sent to the pool, here a boxed closure.
Writing the code you want to call first, then fixing compiler errors until it works.
